data.content_ref: inline:The target's decision rule conflates a synchronic property (empirical content / testability) with a diachronic one (corroboration / past survival), and this conflation is the very induction it disavows. The rule says to 'Select the hypothesis that has withstood the most stringent attempts at refutation.' If the justificatory work is done solely by empirical content — which determines 'opportunities for future error detection' — then past test-survival is irrelevant: one should simply prefer the most testable theory regardless of its history. But the rule explicitly makes *survival of past refutation* the selection criterion, not bare content. Once past survival is load-bearing in the rule, the justification 'thereby offering the best available opportunity for future error detection' projects a past-track-record property into a future-performance claim. That projection is an inductive inference, not merely a procedural imperative. The target cannot have it both ways: either corroboration (past survival) does no justificatory work, in which case Popper's actual preference for corroborated over merely-testable theories is ungrounded on the stated basis; or it does work, in which case the 'no probabilistic claim about the future' defense fails because the rule's forward-looking justification depends on exactly such a projection.
